analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other wealthy countries, with FDA safety checks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was referred to, and died there at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have opened the U.S. market to prescription drugs sold in Australia, Canada, the European Union, Japan, New Zealand, and Switzerland. Americans could buy from registered, FDA-inspected foreign pharmacies—by mail for personal use or through U.S. wholesalers and pharmacies—rather than paying the much higher prices charged only in the United States. It paired that with a strict safety regime: registered importers and exporters, verified chains of custody, facility inspections, shipment tracking, and recalls. It also barred drug manufacturers from punishing exporters with higher prices or supply cutoffs. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially those paying out of pocket for brand-name drugs: they could buy the same FDA-approved medicines from registered pharmacies in countries where prices run 35 to 55 percent lower, with a 90-day personal-import limit. U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers that registered as importers would gain a new supply channel, and consumers would gain protection against manufacturers cutting off foreign supply or price-discriminating against importers.

how_it_helps.text: It waives the current ban on importing foreign-made prescription drugs, letting registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals buy qualifying drugs from Australia, Canada, the EU, Japan, New Zealand, and Switzerland, where the bill's findings note prices run 35 to 55 percent lower.

It bans manufacturer discrimination—charging exporters more than local buyers, cutting off supply, or otherwise restricting importation—and makes resale of properly sold foreign drugs lawful rather than patent infringement.

It builds safety in: registered importers and exporters must be inspected, verify chains of custody from the manufacturer, mark shipments with anti-counterfeit tracking, and post bonds; the FDA can refuse any shipment that looks counterfeit, tampered, or unsafe, and the FTC can act against discriminatory practices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. profits depend on charging Americans more than the same drugs sell for in Canada, Europe, and other wealthy countries. They would face new legal restrictions on price-discriminating against importers, restricting supply to exporters, and making their foreign versions differ from U.S. versions.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs may differ from U.S.-approved versions in inactive ingredients or manufacturing process, and the FDA itself has long warned that verifying safety of drugs sold abroad is difficult; the bill's inspection and chain-of-custody regime mitigates but cannot eliminate this risk.

The bill permits foreign distributors to sell to Americans only for personal use (up to a 90-day supply), which helps individuals but would not automatically change the opaque pricing system inside the U.S., and manufacturers could find ways to constrain foreign supply within the limits of the bill's anti-discrimination rules.

The registration and inspection regime—bonds, fees, 12 annual inspections per registrant, shipment marking—adds compliance costs that would be passed on to consumers in some measure, though the bill caps inspection fees at 2.5 percent of import value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits, the bill offered real price relief for a genuine burden—American prescription prices are far above those of peer countries—and it tried to answer the safety objection with a serious verification regime rather than pretending the risks away. The drawbacks are real: supply chains are global, and a committed exporter or manufacturer could still slip noncompliant product past inspections; the manufacturer could also partially blunt savings by restricting sales to Canada. But weighed against the $200+ billion Americans spend annually on prescriptions, the potential savings were large, and the safety risks were addressed, not ignored. The bill's failure means none of that was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee when introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Introduced February 10, 2011, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

No further action was ever recorded: the bill sat in committee for the full two-year Congress without a hearing, a committee vote, or a Senate floor vote, and expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

It had 21 cosponsors alongside its sponsor—16 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 1 Independent—a bipartisan roster that included both party leadership figures and members of both parties, yet the committee still took no action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who kept the import ban in place and their freedom to charge Americans higher prices than the same drugs sell for abroad.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Cosponsors including Sens. McCain, Grassley, Stabenow, Klobuchar, Sanders, Kerry, and Leahy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties including senior members of both parties.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation legislation, which it has long campaigned against on safety grounds; such opposition is a well-known feature of every importation bill fight, though it appears nowhere in the congressional record on this bill.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (no chairman action recorded)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—despite its bipartisan sponsor roster.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan—21 cosponsors split 16 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 1 Independent, led by a Republican sponsor—so the bill's death in committee cannot be attributed to one party. It never reached a roll call.

industries.note: The bill opens their most profitable market to price competition from the same drugs sold cheaper abroad and bars them from cutting off or discriminating against exporters. It directly attacks the price segmentation that keeps U.S. prices the highest in the world.

Pharmacies and wholesalers could become registered importers and profit from cheaper supply, but the $10,000 registration fee, inspection fees, and compliance burdens fall on them, and they compete with direct-to-consumer imports from exporters.

industries.industry: Registered internet pharmacies and exporters (especially Canadian)
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, FDA-registered channel for cross-border online pharmacies that currently operate in a gray zone, with a public list of approved exporters so consumers can find them.

industries.industry: Payment processors and credit card networks
industries.note: The bill bars payment systems from processing transactions with unregistered foreign pharmacies, a compliance mandate for an industry that today processes such payments without restriction.
